topic: Why Bhutan Is Stranger Than You Think
hook: Your watch gains thirty minutes when you walk through one gate in Jaigaon, and nobody stops you.
title: Why Bhutan Is Stranger Than You Think
description:
Walk through Bhutan Gate in Jaigaon and you step from India into Phuentsholing, Bhutan, with a 30-minute time jump and no wall in between. This video covers seven true facts about Bhutan: its time zone, its forests, Gross National Happiness, the late arrival of TV, a capital with no traffic lights, the Paro airport, and a mountain no one has climbed.

#Bhutan #GeographyFacts #StrangePlaces
tags: Why Bhutan is stranger than you think
comment_prompt: Which Bhutan fact surprised you most?

scenes.narration: Your watch gains thirty minutes when you walk through one gate in Jaigaon, and nobody stops you.
scenes.headline: One Gate, +30 Minutes

scenes.narration: That gate leads from India into Bhutan, a country with no traffic lights in its capital and a ban on climbing its mountains.
scenes.headline: Welcome To Bhutan

scenes.narration: By the end, you will see a mountain nobody has ever climbed, and why the rule keeping it that way is so strict.
scenes.headline: The Unclimbed Peak

scenes.narration: But first, we start at the gate, because it is one of the strangest border crossings you can walk in a minute.
scenes.headline: Start At The Gate

scenes.narration: Stay with me, because every fact here is a little stranger than the one before it.
scenes.headline: Each One Stranger

scenes.narration: Chapter one. In West Bengal, the Indian town of Jaigaon sits right beside the Bhutanese town of Phuentsholing.
scenes.headline: Jaigaon Meets Phuentsholing

scenes.narration: The line between them is a gate, called Bhutan Gate. Walk through it on foot and you have left India.
scenes.headline: Walk Out Of India

scenes.narration: There is no river and no wall. The streets and shops simply carry on, on the other side of the arch.
scenes.headline: No Wall, No River

scenes.narration: Indian citizens do not need a visa for Bhutan. They need an entry permit, which can be collected at the border.
scenes.headline: No Visa For Indians

scenes.narration: Even your money works. Bhutan's ngultrum is tied one to one with the Indian rupee, and rupees are widely accepted.
scenes.headline: Rupees Work Here

scenes.narration: So you can pay in rupees, in a different country, a few steps from where you started.
scenes.headline: Pay In Rupees Abroad

scenes.narration: Phuentsholing is the main road gateway into Bhutan. From here, travellers begin the long drive up into the mountains to Thimphu.
scenes.headline: The Road Gateway

scenes.narration: Many visitors say the Bhutanese side feels calmer and cleaner within minutes of crossing. Same street level, different feeling.
scenes.headline: Same Street, New Feel

scenes.narration: Chapter two. Bhutan runs on a time that is thirty minutes ahead of Indian Standard Time.
scenes.headline: Thirty Minutes Ahead

scenes.narration: India sits at plus five thirty from universal time. Bhutan sits at plus six. One gate, one half hour.
scenes.headline: +5:30 vs +6:00

scenes.narration: So a phone that updates itself can jump forward by half an hour while you are buying a cup of tea.
scenes.headline: Your Phone Jumps

scenes.narration: The same time on a wall clock can mean two different moments, depending on which side of the arch you stand.
scenes.headline: Two Moments, One Street

scenes.narration: Nepal has its own odd offset too, forty-five minutes past the hour, but Bhutan's is a clean half hour.
scenes.headline: Nepal Is +5:45

scenes.narration: That was the mild one. The next fact is about how Bhutan treats its forests.
scenes.headline: Next: The Forests

scenes.narration: Chapter three. Bhutan takes in more carbon dioxide than it releases. It calls itself carbon negative.
scenes.headline: Carbon Negative

scenes.narration: Most countries cannot say that. Bhutan can, mainly because forests cover most of its land.
scenes.headline: Forest Covers Most

scenes.narration: Its constitution says at least sixty percent of the country must stay under forest cover.
scenes.headline: 60% Must Stay Forest

scenes.narration: That is not a slogan on a poster. It is written into the highest law of the land.
scenes.headline: Written Into Law

scenes.narration: Those forests are home to tigers, red pandas and snow leopards, animals most people only meet in documentaries.
scenes.headline: Tigers And Red Pandas

scenes.narration: Bhutan also makes electricity from hydropower, using fast rivers that rush down from the Himalayas.
scenes.headline: Power From Rivers

scenes.narration: It even sells extra power to India, so some lights in Indian homes run on Bhutanese rivers.
scenes.headline: Bhutan Powers India

scenes.narration: A small mountain kingdom is helping to power its giant neighbour, and it all connects back to that little gate.
scenes.headline: Small Land, Big Help

scenes.narration: Now something more personal. Bhutan measures how happy its people are, and it does so on purpose.
scenes.headline: Counting Happiness

scenes.narration: Chapter four. Most countries track money. Bhutan also tracks happiness, and calls it Gross National Happiness.
scenes.headline: Gross National Happiness

scenes.narration: The idea is linked to the fourth king of Bhutan, who talked about it in the 1970s.
scenes.headline: A King's Idea

scenes.narration: He said happiness matters more than gross national product. That was a bold thing for a king to say.
scenes.headline: Happiness Over GDP

scenes.narration: Today the government looks at health, education, time use, culture and a healthy environment, not only income.
scenes.headline: More Than Income

scenes.narration: Policies are meant to be checked against this idea, not just against how much money they make.
scenes.headline: Policies Get Checked

scenes.narration: That does not make everyone happy. Many young Bhutanese leave to find work abroad, and the country knows it.
scenes.headline: Not A Perfect Story

scenes.narration: But the idea is real, and very few countries put it at the centre of their planning.
scenes.headline: A Rare Idea

scenes.narration: Even the national sport, archery, feels more like a festival, with teams, singing and dancing at the matches.
scenes.headline: Archery Is A Party

scenes.narration: If you like strange places and facts that sound fake, subscribe, because there is plenty more like this coming.
scenes.headline: Subscribe For More

scenes.narration: Bhutan also opened up to the world very late. Until 1999, there was no television in the country at all.
scenes.headline: No TV Until 1999

scenes.narration: Think about that. India already had cable channels in the nineties, while Bhutan was still living without a screen.
scenes.headline: India Had Cable

scenes.narration: In 1999 the king allowed television and the internet, and Bhutan became one of the last countries to get TV.
scenes.headline: TV Finally Arrives

scenes.narration: Leaders worried what a flood of foreign shows would do to local culture and old traditions.
scenes.headline: Worry About Culture

scenes.narration: Imagine the first village evening when a glowing screen switched on in a room that had never seen one.
scenes.headline: The First Screen

scenes.narration: Today many Bhutanese understand Hindi, partly thanks to Bollywood films and Indian channels.
scenes.headline: Bollywood In Bhutan

scenes.narration: Which makes the next fact feel even stranger, because it is about the roads of the capital.
scenes.headline: Next: The Roads

scenes.narration: Chapter five. Thimphu, the capital of Bhutan, has no traffic lights.
scenes.headline: Zero Traffic Lights

scenes.narration: Reports say lights were tried once in the late nineties, and people did not like them.
scenes.headline: Lights Were Tried

scenes.narration: They were taken away, and a police officer went back to directing cars by hand.
scenes.headline: Back To Hand Signals

scenes.narration: An officer stands at a junction, raising his arms and turning his body to guide every car.
scenes.headline: A Human Signal

scenes.narration: Visitors film it like a performance. It is a job, a tourist stop and a traffic system, all at once.
scenes.headline: Tourists Film It

scenes.narration: It works because Thimphu is small, with far fewer cars than cities like Delhi or Mumbai.
scenes.headline: Small City, Few Cars

scenes.narration: Picture your own city with no signals, no wall of honking, and one person in charge of the whole junction.
scenes.headline: Imagine Your City

scenes.narration: Bhutan also keeps tourism small with a daily fee, which has been 1,200 rupees per night for Indian visitors.
scenes.headline: A Daily Visitor Fee

scenes.narration: Chapter six. Paro is Bhutan's only international airport, and it sits in a deep valley between high peaks.
scenes.headline: Paro Airport

scenes.narration: Pilots cannot simply line up and land as they do at Delhi. They must follow a curved path between mountains.
scenes.headline: Curving Between Peaks

scenes.narration: Only a small group of specially trained pilots can land here, and it is known as one of the hardest airports.
scenes.headline: Special Pilots Only

scenes.narration: Flights here depend on daylight and good weather, because there is almost no room for a mistake.
scenes.headline: Daylight And Clear Sky

scenes.narration: From the window you can see houses, rice fields and monasteries close enough to count.
scenes.headline: Houses From The Window

scenes.narration: Bhutan's national airline is Drukair, and Druk means thunder dragon.
scenes.headline: Druk Means Dragon

scenes.narration: Bhutan's own name for itself is Druk Yul, the land of the thunder dragon.
scenes.headline: Land Of Thunder Dragon

scenes.narration: Those peaks around the airport are high, but the biggest one in Bhutan is stranger than all of them.
scenes.headline: The Biggest One

scenes.narration: Chapter seven, the one I promised. Bhutan has a mountain that no human has ever climbed.
scenes.headline: Never Climbed

scenes.narration: It is called Gangkhar Puensum, and at about seven thousand five hundred metres, it is the highest unclimbed mountain on Earth.
scenes.headline: Gangkhar Puensum

scenes.narration: A few expeditions tried in the 1980s. None of them reached the top.
scenes.headline: Attempts Failed

scenes.narration: Then in 1994 Bhutan banned climbing its highest peaks, and in 2003 it banned mountaineering altogether.
scenes.headline: Climbing Banned

scenes.narration: The reason is spiritual. Many Bhutanese believe mountains are homes of gods and spirits, and should not be stepped on.
scenes.headline: Homes Of Spirits

scenes.narration: That means no permits, no base camp and no summit photo, as long as the rule stands.
scenes.headline: No Base Camp

scenes.narration: Almost anywhere else, a peak this high would have a queue of climbers and a line of tents.
scenes.headline: Elsewhere It Would Be Busy

scenes.narration: Instead it sits in clean snow, with no flags and no footprints, because a whole country chose to say no.
scenes.headline: A Country Said No

scenes.narration: So look again at that gate in Jaigaon. A few steps, no wall, and you enter a country that bans climbing a mountain.
scenes.headline: Back To The Gate

scenes.narration: A capital with no traffic lights, a thirty minute time jump, and a constitution that protects its forests.
scenes.headline: All Behind One Gate

scenes.narration: All of it begins at a gate you can walk through in under a minute.
scenes.headline: Under A Minute

scenes.narration: Your watch gains thirty minutes at the gate in Jaigaon, and a country that does things its own way is waiting beyond it.
scenes.headline: Your Watch Gains 30

scenes.narration: Next in this series: another country that is stranger than you think. Follow along so you do not miss it.
scenes.headline: Up Next
